summary.text: A factorial, written n!, counts the distinct sequences, called permutations, of n distinct objects.
Arranging n distinct objects into a sequence can be done in n factorial ways, and the factorial of zero is defined to be 1.
Factorials appear in ancient Indian and Jewish writings, and Christian Kramp introduced the exclamation-mark notation in 1808.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: Factorials grow more quickly than exponential growth

facts.label: Pacioli's table
facts.value: In 1494 he calculated factorials up to 11!

facts.label: Bell ringing
facts.value: Fabian Stedman applied factorials to change ringing in 1677

items.prompt: A librarian wants to know how many different orders five different books can take on a shelf. Which number gives that?

options.label: 5 × 5, since any book can go in any spot
5, one for each book
5!, the factorial of 5
5 + 5, one for each end of the shelf

items.explain: The factorial n! counts the ways of arranging n distinct objects into a sequence.

items.prompt: A shelf holds no books at all. How many ways are there to arrange the books on it?

options.label: Zero ways, since there is nothing to arrange
Exactly one way, doing nothing
Two ways, empty or not empty
No answer, because it makes no sense

items.explain: With nothing to permute, the only rearrangement is to do nothing, so there is exactly one permutation of zero objects, matching 0! = 1.

items.prompt: You choose 2 friends out of 5 for a team and the order of choosing does not matter. Why do factorials appear in the formula for such counts?

options.label: They account for different orderings of the objects
They make the numbers in the formula smaller
They count only the even numbered friends
They are needed only when a group has five members

items.explain: Factorials appear broadly in combinatorics to account for different orderings of objects.

items.prompt: Why is the factorial called by that name?

options.label: Because it was invented to factor large numbers
Because it is only defined for prime numbers
Because it factors an exponential into smaller powers
Because the terms of its product formula are its factors

items.explain: The word refers to the terms of the product formula for the factorial, which are its factors.

items.prompt: A church team has several tuned bells and wants to ring them in every possible order without repeating one. Which tool counts those orders?

options.label: A binomial coefficient, which counts subsets
A factorial, which counts orderings
A power series for the exponential function
A prime factorization of the number of bells

items.explain: Factorials count the ways to order distinct objects, and Fabian Stedman applied them to change ringing, the ringing of several tuned bells.

items.prompt: A programmer computes factorials by repeating the rule that n! is n times the factorial of the number just below it. Why does defining 0! as 1 help?

options.label: It makes every answer an even number
It lets the rule stop at one and avoid zero
Only zero is needed as a starting value, with no special cases
It makes factorials of large numbers faster to compute

items.explain: With 0! = 1 the recurrence stays valid at 1, so a recursive computation needs only the value at zero as its base case.
